title: Guardian Reports Dispute Over Wiretap Claim in Pentagon Leak Inquiry
description_short: The Guardian reported conflicting accounts about a claimed warrantless wiretap during the Pentagon’s leak inquiry.
description_medium: The Guardian reported that Pete Hegseth’s lawyer, Tim Parlatore, initially suggested investigators found a warrantless wiretap on an aide’s phone, then denied one occurred. White House advisers said they viewed the claim as untrue, and the inquiry was later transferred to Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg. This documents a disputed account, not a knowingly false statement by Hegseth or his lawyer.
description_long: The Guardian reported on May 27, 2025, that conflicting accounts emerged during a Pentagon investigation into classified-information leaks. Advisers told the paper that Tim Parlatore, Pete Hegseth’s personal lawyer and a supervisor of the inquiry, suggested investigators had found a warrantless wiretap on an aide’s phone. The report said Parlatore later denied that a wiretap occurred, while White House advisers viewed his claim as untrue. It also said the inquiry moved to Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg’s office around the time Parlatore planned to step away. The article described competing statements and a change in who oversaw the investigation. It does not establish that Hegseth or Parlatore knowingly lied; the reporting describes a disputed claim, not proof of either person’s knowledge or intent. The account concerns how the leak inquiry was handled and the unresolved dispute over whether a wiretap had been found.
subcategory: Pentagon leak investigation and disputed wiretap account
organization_tags: Air Force Office of Special Investigations

title: DOJ Establishes $1.776 Billion Anti-Weaponization Fund After Trump IRS Settlement
description_short: DOJ created a $1.776 billion claims fund after settling Trump’s IRS lawsuit; no payouts were reported by May 2026.
description_medium: In May 2026, the Justice Department announced a $1.776 billion Anti-Weaponization Fund following settlement of Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the IRS over disclosure of his tax records. DOJ said a five-member commission would review claims from people alleging government weaponization. The fund faced legal challenges, and CNN reported that no payments had been made by May 22.
description_long: On May 18, 2026, the Justice Department announced a $1.776 billion Anti-Weaponization Fund after the settlement of Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service over disclosure of his tax records. DOJ said a five-member commission appointed by the attorney general would review applications from people who allege that federal agencies improperly targeted them. The department described the fund as a remedy for government weaponization. Critics challenged its legality and argued that broad eligibility criteria could benefit political allies. CNN reported on May 22 that lawsuits sought to block the fund and that no payments had yet been made. The settlement of Trump’s tax-record suit is the context for the announcement; it does not determine whether other applicants were improperly targeted. The cited reports establish the fund’s announced amount and review process, the legal challenges, and the absence of payments as of May 22. They do not establish a payment to any applicant or an exchange for clemency or political support.

title: Court Ordered Acosta’s Press Pass Restored After Due-Process Finding
description_short: Judge Timothy Kelly temporarily ordered Acosta’s hard pass restored after finding a likely Fifth Amendment due-process violation; he did not decide the First Amendment claim.
description_medium: After the White House revoked Jim Acosta’s press pass in November 2018, CNN and Acosta sued. At the November 16 hearing, Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the pass restored temporarily, finding Acosta was likely deprived of Fifth Amendment due-process protections because he received no notice or opportunity to respond. The court did not decide the First Amendment claim; the White House later restored the pass permanently.
description_long: After the White House revoked CNN correspondent Jim Acosta’s press pass following a November 7, 2018, news conference, CNN and Acosta filed suit. At a November 16 hearing, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly granted temporary relief and ordered the White House to restore Acosta’s hard pass. The hearing transcript shows Kelly’s reasoning focused on the likelihood that Acosta had been deprived of Fifth Amendment due-process protections because the government had not given him advance notice or an opportunity to respond before revoking his access. The judge did not decide the First Amendment question, and the temporary order was not a final ruling that the White House violated both amendments. Reuters reported on November 19 that the White House made a final decision to restore the credentials, ending the immediate court dispute. The hearing addressed notice and an opportunity to respond before press access was revoked. The supplied sources do not establish that a particular edited video was the sole basis for revoking the pass.

title: Trump Order Exempted Listed Federal Agencies from Labor-Relations Statutes
description_short: A March 2025 order exempted specified federal agencies and components from federal labor-management relations programs.
description_medium: President Trump’s March 27, 2025 executive order excluded listed agencies and agency subdivisions from federal labor-management relations statutes, invoking national-security authority. The Office of Personnel Management’s implementation memo identifies covered organizations. The order changed labor-relations coverage for the listed federal units; it did not eliminate unions or collective bargaining across federal, state and private employment.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14251, titled “Exclusions From Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs,” on March 27, 2025. The order invokes statutory authority to exempt listed federal agencies and agency subdivisions from the Federal Service and Foreign Service labor-management statutes. An Office of Personnel Management implementation memorandum states that covered organizations are no longer required to collectively bargain with federal unions and that unions lose exclusive-recognition status for those covered units. The order therefore materially changes bargaining rights for named federal components. Its legal scope is the listed federal agencies and subdivisions; it does not eliminate unions or bargaining across all public and private employment. The executive order also includes mechanisms for agency heads to identify further qualifying subdivisions under its terms. The supplied Project 2025 and labor-group sources provide policy context, but the official order and OPM memo establish what was enacted. This account replaces the original claim of complete union elimination with the documented federal-sector change and keeps the policy’s limited coverage clear.

The collective bargaining ban included directing NLRB to prosecute union leaders for political advocacy while allowing employers to negotiate away overtime protections, workplace safety requirements, and fair scheduling in exchange for token benefits that reduced worker power and economic security. Trump's union elimination violated fundamental worker rights by destroying legal protections that had enabled collective action while creating 'union-free' environment where workers faced employer retaliation without legal recourse or organizational support to address workplace abuse, wage theft, and unsafe conditions. The worker rights destruction created what labor advocates called systematic return to 'Gilded Age' exploitation where employers gained complete control over working conditions while eliminating worker voice in workplace decisions, economic security, and safety protections that unions had historically provided through collective bargaining. The complete union elimination represented Project 2025's vision of labor relations controlled by corporate interests rather than worker rights, transforming employment from protected relationship with collective bargaining into 'at-will' system where workers lacked voice, representation, or legal protection against employer abuse and exploitation through systematic elimination of labor organizing and collective action.

title: Trump Accused Arizona Officials of Stealing Election Amid 2022 Tabulator Problems
description_short: Trump said Arizona officials were trying to steal the election as Maricopa County reported ballot-machine problems.
description_medium: On November 8, 2022, Donald Trump posted that Maricopa County machines were not counting ballots and said officials were trying to steal the election. Reuters and NBC reported printer and tabulator problems at some vote centers; Maricopa County later documented the equipment issues and ballot-handling procedures. The sources establish the malfunction and Trump’s accusation, not fraud or altered votes.
description_long: On Election Day, November 8, 2022, Maricopa County reported problems with ballot-on-demand printers and tabulators at some vote centers. Donald Trump responded in a Truth Social post, telling Arizonans not to leave before voting and claiming officials were trying to steal the election with faulty machines and delays. Reuters and NBC reported the equipment problems and the election-fraud claims that followed. Maricopa County’s post-election report describes the printer and tabulator issues and how affected ballots were handled, including directing some voters to use another tabulator or place ballots in secure boxes for later counting. These sources support the existence of operational problems and Trump’s attributed accusation. They do not show that votes were changed or that the election was stolen. Trump posted before the midterm races were called, so this statement preceded the results rather than responding to candidates’ losses.

description_long: On March 6, 2015, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network announced a $10 million civil money penalty against Trump Taj Mahal Casino Resort for willful and repeated Bank Secrecy Act violations. FinCEN said the casino admitted violations involving its anti-money-laundering program, reporting duties, and recordkeeping requirements. The agency also described earlier compliance problems, including a $477,700 civil penalty it assessed in 1998 for currency-transaction-reporting violations. The 2015 action followed a history of warnings and required corrective measures identified by the agency. The Bank Secrecy Act requires casinos to maintain anti-money-laundering programs and report specified financial activity; FinCEN’s assessment describes failures in those controls and obligations. FinCEN’s assessment specifies the civil penalty and the regulatory duties at issue. It is an administrative enforcement action and does not constitute a criminal conviction. The cited records do not establish political motive or prove that every transaction at the casino was unlawful; they document the agency’s findings and the casino’s admission of the described violations.

description_short: Court filings and a congressional report documented foreign-government-linked spending at Trump properties and emoluments allegations.
description_medium: An amended complaint in the D.C. and Maryland case cited Saudi-agent disclosures reporting payments to Trump’s Washington hotel. A House Oversight report, issued by Democratic committee members and based on a limited set of Mazars records, identified at least $7.8 million in payments from 20 foreign governments to Trump businesses during his presidency. The plaintiffs alleged violations of the Foreign Emoluments Clause; the records establish payments and allegations, not a court finding of unconstitutionality.
description_long: An amended complaint filed by the attorneys general of the District of Columbia and Maryland cited foreign-agent disclosures reporting payments by an agent for Saudi Arabia to the Trump International Hotel in Washington. It listed $190,272 for lodging, $78,204 for catering and $1,568 for parking during a six-month period spanning October 2016 through March 2017, and alleged that some payments came after Trump’s inauguration. Separately, a House Oversight report based on Mazars accounting records identified at least $7.8 million in payments from 20 foreign governments to Trump businesses during his presidency. The report was issued by Democratic committee members and described a limited portion of records. The D.C. and Maryland plaintiffs argued that foreign-government-linked payments violated the Foreign Emoluments Clause. The complaint records allegations and the House report describes payments in its reviewed records; neither, on its own, establishes a final constitutional merits ruling. These sources support an attributed account of spending and litigation, not a categorical claim that the Constitution was violated.
